title: Gleaning (Ruth 2–4)
hook: Boaz leaves extra grain on purpose, and Ruth becomes David's great-grandmother

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ruth on the road to Bethlehem: whither thou goest, I will go. Your line was thy people, my people. Who did you stay with a little longer? Day three hundred ninety-six.

There's no food in the house. Naomi and Ruth have reached Bethlehem with nothing, just as the barley harvest begins. So Ruth does what the poor did in Israel. She goes out to a field behind the reapers and picks up what they drop. The law of Moses said farmers must not strip their fields bare: leave the edges, leave what falls, for the poor and the stranger. It was a safety net, built into the harvest. Ruth is both poor and a stranger. And the field she happens to walk into belongs to a man named Boaz, Booz in the Douay-Rheims, a relative of Naomi's dead husband. Today's word is what she does there all day.
screen: `NO FOOD IN THE HOUSE.` → `LEAVE THE EDGES FOR THE POOR.` → `A FIELD THAT BELONGS TO BOAZ.`

segments.voice: Gleaning means gathering what's left after the harvest: the stray ears of grain, the leftovers, the edges. It's slow, bent-over work, and it's the work of people with nothing else. Boaz walks out, sees the foreign woman, and asks who she is. He's already heard: everything she did for her mother-in-law has been told to him. So he protects her. Stay in my field, drink from my workers' water jars, eat with us at mealtime. Then, when she goes back to work, he quietly tells his young men this, in the Douay: "let fall some of your handfuls of purpose, and leave them, that she may gather them without shame." Of purpose. He doesn't hand her a sack of grain like a charity case. He arranges the field so her own work finds more, and her dignity stays whole. That evening she beats out what she gathered and has about an ephah of barley. In the chapters that follow, Naomi sends Ruth to Boaz at the threshing floor, and Boaz acts as the go'el, the kinsman who redeems a family's land and name. He marries Ruth. They have a son, Obed. And the book ends with a short family tree: Obed is the father of Jesse, and Jesse the father of David. A foreign widow who gathered leftovers becomes the great-grandmother of King David. Catholics hear one more step. When Matthew's Gospel opens with Jesus's family tree, Ruth is named in it, one of only a few women listed. Kindness on purpose, in one barley field, runs all the way to Bethlehem again.
screen: `GLEANING — GATHERING WHAT'S LEFT.` · `LET FALL SOME HANDFULS ON PURPOSE.` · `BOAZ, THE KINSMAN WHO REDEEMS.` · `GREAT-GRANDMOTHER OF DAVID.` · then, large: `THAT SHE MAY GATHER THEM WITHOUT SHAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave extra for someone. Settle, and breathe. Think about where your own field has edges. The extra in the grocery cart. The time after a meeting. The tip. The parking spot near the door. The credit for an idea. Pick one place where you could let something fall on purpose, so someone else can pick it up without feeling handed charity. Picture who that might be. Then picture doing it quietly, the way Boaz did, so nobody has to say thank you. If you pray, you can ask for eyes like his. The bell holds the time.
Gleaning. Gathering the grain left behind after harvest, which the law left for the poor and the stranger. Ruth gleaned in the field of Boaz. Today's word.
Your line: kindness on purpose. Today, leave one handful for someone, and don't tell them you did. Day three hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Ruth's story in the weekday Mass readings, and some Catholic charities and parish food ministries point to gleaning as a model of caring for the poor while protecting their dignity.

fork.setup: you're Boaz. a foreign widow is gleaning in your field, and you've heard how faithful she's been to her mother-in-law. what do you do?

give her a full sack of grain at the gate.
tell your workers to drop extra on purpose for her to find.
fork.reveal: he protects her, feeds her, and has his men let fall handfuls on purpose, "that she may gather them without shame." help that keeps her dignity whole.

original.note: Hebrew: redeemer, the near kinsman who buys back a family's land and carries on its name. Boaz acts as Ruth's go'el.

trapdoor: what you thought: gleaning is an old word for collecting information.
what it means: gleaning was gathering what the reapers left, a right the law gave the poor and the stranger. Boaz made sure Ruth found more.
what a scholar hears: Leviticus 19 and Deuteronomy 24 command leaving the gleanings; Ruth's story ends with a genealogy running from Obed to David.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens like day 395's ('Three widows' / 'Two widows'); 'Israel's greatest king' cut to 'King David'; 'often' in howItsDone softened.
Gleaning laws (Leviticus 19:9–10; 23:22; Deuteronomy 24:19–21) summarized as leaving edges and fallen grain for the poor and the stranger; confirm.
Ephah of barley (Ruth 2:17; the Douay glosses it as about three bushels): kept as 'about an ephah'.
The threshing floor scene (Ruth 3) is mentioned only briefly and delicately; confirm the Keeper is comfortable with that.
Matthew's genealogy names a few women (Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, the wife of Uriah, and Mary); 'one of only a few women listed' is meant to cover this.
howItsDone: the claim about Catholic charities citing gleaning is general; confirm or soften.
